reverse_outline.summary: Chapter aim: how search, navigation, merchandising, recommendations and reviews help a shopper find a product, and what catalog, prices and stock must provide.
Key points: the index is a copy that goes stale; search is only as good as the data under it; reviews are discovery data with provenance rules.
Failure patterns addressed: the Phantom Stock, the Message in a Bottle and the Lynchpin, each as it appears in search.
A jacket vanishes from filtered results because its waterproof rating never reached the storefront; discovery depends on product facts, not ranking.
The search index only holds copies of content, price and stock; copies age, so each feed needs a named source and a repair process.
Reviews are the fourth kind of index data: a ranking signal that also carries a legally required record of where each review came from.
Roadmap of the chapter: the Kestrel & Pine report, discovery vocabulary, the index as a copy, reviews, product choices, and failures.
Topics left to other chapters and the companion book: source data owners, deep engine and ranking detail, shopping agents, SEO.
Places the chapter in the order's journey: Eva searches for a jacket, and search must combine description, price and stock.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Setting the Scene at Kestrel & Pine: The Waterproof Jacket Nobody Could Find ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: Sets up Kestrel & Pine's March 2027 search review: built-in search, catalog size, who took part, figures illustrative.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Setting the Scene at Kestrel & Pine: The Waterproof Jacket Nobody Could Find ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: What the report showed: the best-seller unfindable for lack of an attribute, no synonyms, and two-hour-old stock shown on the busiest evening.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Setting the Scene at Kestrel & Pine: The Waterproof Jacket Nobody Could Find ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: The three fixes: synonym sets now, a waterproofness attribute when the PIM arrives, and availability from its own service later.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Three Ways to Find a Product ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: Discovery is whatever connects a shopper's need to the roughly 17,000 active variants.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Three Ways to Find a Product ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: Plain definitions of search terms: index, indexing, relevance, ranking, facet, merchandising rule, synonym set, typo tolerance, personalization, zero-result rate.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Three Ways to Find a Product ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: Baymard's research shows sites handle product-name searches but often fail feature and use-case queries, the same pattern as Kestrel & Pine.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: How the Pieces Fit Together: The Index as a Copy ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: Introduces the diagram: the search service consumes four systems of record, each changing at its own pace.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: How the Pieces Fit Together: The Index as a Copy ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: The central decision is which facts sit in the index (filterable but stale) and which are fetched fresh at query time (current but not filterable).

reverse_outline.draft_locator: How the Pieces Fit Together: The Index as a Copy ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: The rule behind the table: each feed must refresh as often as the shown statement can change; otherwise fetch the fact at query time.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: How the Pieces Fit Together: The Index as a Copy ¶4
reverse_outline.summary: Availability is the hardest case: chained stock copies showed sold-out items as in stock; the fix is a coarse event-fed flag plus a live check.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: How the Pieces Fit Together: The Index as a Copy ¶5
reverse_outline.summary: Scheduled synchronization copies on an interval, so the index lags by that interval or more.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: How the Pieces Fit Together: The Index as a Copy ¶6
reverse_outline.summary: Event-driven indexing updates records within seconds but needs safe handling of repeats and a job that finds missed updates.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: How the Pieces Fit Together: The Index as a Copy ¶7
reverse_outline.summary: Always keep a full rebuild possible, built beside the live index and switched over only when complete.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: How the Pieces Fit Together: The Index as a Copy ¶8
reverse_outline.summary: How a lexical engine matches and ranks words, and why synonyms applied at search time are easier to keep current.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: How the Pieces Fit Together: The Index as a Copy ¶9
reverse_outline.summary: Merchandising rules override relevance and should be managed like promotions, with an owner, start, end and regular review.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: How the Pieces Fit Together: The Index as a Copy ¶10
reverse_outline.summary: Facets are only as good as attribute completeness and platform limits, so their quality is decided in the PIM.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: How the Pieces Fit Together: The Index as a Copy ¶11
reverse_outline.summary: Collaborative filtering recommends from other shoppers' behaviour; Amazon's history shows simple baselines are hard to beat.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: How the Pieces Fit Together: The Index as a Copy ¶12
reverse_outline.summary: Vector search matches meaning, and hybrid search merges it with word matching; major engines now offer it because word matching alone misses variants.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: How the Pieces Fit Together: The Index as a Copy ¶13
reverse_outline.summary: Embeddings are another derived copy that goes stale and needs reindexing on a model change / Vendor conversion-lift figures are uncontrolled anecdotes, so measure your own first.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: How the Pieces Fit Together: The Index as a Copy ¶14
reverse_outline.summary: Conversational search is the frontier, and what an assistant needs from the merchant is the same structured, fresh data agents need.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: How the Pieces Fit Together: The Index as a Copy ¶15
reverse_outline.summary: Wholesale search must show each buyer their assortment and price; contract prices go in the index for few tiers or are merged at query time for many.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: How the Pieces Fit Together: The Index as a Copy ¶16
reverse_outline.summary: Assortment visibility must be enforced inside the search service, tied to the account's credential, because results can leak information.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Reviews and Ratings as Discovery and Trust Data ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: A review does two jobs: it ranks and persuades as discovery data, and it is a regulated claim of purchase as trust data.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Reviews and Ratings as Discovery and Trust Data ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: EU and US law require merchants to verify that reviews are genuine, disclose ranking parameters, and forbid fake, bought or suppressed reviews.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Reviews and Ratings as Discovery and Trust Data ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: Four design consequences for reviews: record provenance per review, moderate by rule, disclose unconditional incentives, document ranking parameters.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Reviews and Ratings as Discovery and Trust Data ¶4
reverse_outline.summary: Marketplace reviews belong to the marketplaces, not the merchant / A merchant this size should use a specialist reviews service and ensure ratings reach the index and order links survive.
Option one: the shop platform's built-in search, free with published limits, suited to catalogs that fit the platform and tolerate its delay.
Option two: a hosted search service fed by events, buying tooling at the cost of integrations, fees and vendor-held configuration.
Option three: a self-run engine, right when relevance is a competitive asset or data must stay in-house, at the cost of a dedicated team.
Option four: search as its own platform inside a composable or marketplace stack, suited to groups.
The author's rule: measure zero-result rate and failing queries before buying, since much is fixed with existing tools and data.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Across Scale Stages: When It Fits and When It Limits ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: Across scale stages the feeding pipeline matters more than the engine; each stage has a different limiting factor and fix.
Search interfaces get retired by vendors, so integrations must move before the cutoff.
Vendor search limits are documented and can exclude filters, prices or variants, so read them before committing.
Measure search by results found, clicks and purchases per language and channel, keeping counting rules consistent.
Kestrel & Pine's 2027 plan kept its existing vendor, applied the three fixes plus routine upkeep, and cut zero-result searches cheaply.
Failure: the index shows stock the warehouse lacks; how to detect it by sampling and recover with the flag and live check.
Failure: a catalog change never reaches the index; detect with an hourly comparison job and re-index the differences.
Failure: an unplanned full rebuild done in place serves a half-built index; build beside the old one and swap.
Failure: synonyms applied to the wrong language index; detect per-language metrics and keep one owned set per language.
Failure: a merchandising rule outlives its campaign; list rules without end dates and require validity windows.
Failure: review provenance is lost when the reviews app changes; keep the order link in your own store.
Failure: wholesale assortments or prices leak because filtering happened in the storefront; enforce it in the service and treat as a security incident.
Failure: the hosted search service is down; navigation must still work and the search box must show an error, not empty results.
Synthesis: every fault was results unsupported by their sources; three conditions prevent it, all owned outside search, so fund data before a vendor.
What is established: the index is a lagging copy, the standard search measures, hybrid retrieval is now common, and review provenance is legally required.
What depends on context: when built-in search suffices, when a hosted service pays off, when to index availability, where to enforce wholesale visibility.
The author's view: fund the PIM and availability service before a search vendor, and keep rules and synonyms as versioned data outside vendor consoles.
Ten questions for applying the chapter's lessons to the reader's own company.
Hand-off: search showed Eva the jacket as in stock; the next chapter examines what that availability promise means.

Evidence: it named the Kestrel & Pine report, vendor documentation and the EU and US review rules, but said 'I do not expect measured data or studies', so the usability research (one paragraph) was not predicted; the introduction does not mention it.

The reader named the data gap (title says 'shell jacket', rating in a spreadsheet, search indexes only title, description, type and tags, no synonym) and would check the zero-result rate and top failing queries per language and which fields are indexed, before any new engine. Matches expected.

The reader answered: only a coarse 'available' flag in the index, the exact number from the availability service at query time or on the product page, because an indexed fact is only as fresh as the last indexing run and stock changes by the second; it cited the two-hour 'in stock' case. The reader answered: how each review was collected and the order it is linked to, because Directive (EU) 2019/2161 requires a merchant to be able to show reviews come from real purchasers and to take reasonable steps to check. Matches expected.
